analysis.title: Macro Roadmap: Divergence
key_insights: The 2026 UST sell-off is mostly real-rate driven: 98bp of the 108bp rise in the 10y. GS frames the main driver as a supply/demand imbalance, not credibility concerns.

Supply is not slowing: fiscal deficits stay large, fiscal consolidation looks far-fetched, and AI-related capex is projected above $1tn next year. Demand for long-end Treasuries is lower for reasons GS has discussed before.

US 30y real yield is 3.33%, around the top of the post-2010 range, which GS says looks like an attractive long-term hold. With little obvious catalyst for a reversal, long-term holders have no impetus to go all in, which has kept demand tepid.

Nasdaq has barely moved off its highs despite a 2 standard deviation move in the 10y yield over the past month. If AI investment ROI is expected to be easily double digits, a 50-100bp rise in funding cost does little to slow borrowing. This equity resilience has limited FCI tightening.

The speed of the yield sell-off warrants caution about chasing it over the short term. The longer-term imbalance persists unless AI ROI is repriced lower or the cyclical outlook changes, especially if the K-shaped economy deteriorates more sharply in some areas.

Higher rates hit lower income quartiles, rate-sensitive sectors such as housing, and small businesses harder. Russell 2000 has underperformed NDX in 16 of the last 20 sessions, by about 9pp cumulatively.

GS finds the Fed path extremely tricky to call. The supply/demand story is a long-end story, and US core inflation is already at its peak in GIR's profile, so the cost-of-capital argument implies more term premium. The Fed is wary of higher inflation expectations, and a labour market pickup (now stabilised around GS's breakeven estimate) would be hawkish.
Warsh's reaction function is described as incredibly hard to predict: it is unclear whether he weighs the inflation path or broader FCI more.

AI winners vs losers is also a macro theme. The AI capex boom is US driven but raises the global cost of capital. Higher rates are easier for countries with higher nominal growth, per the r-g equation.

France's r-g is currently about 0, but its marginal financing cost is about 250bp above the effective interest rate on outstanding debt. As debt refinances at current rates, r-g deteriorates and the debt trajectory worsens.

Europe will lag in capturing AI growth benefits. Sovereign spread widening can tighten FCI further, energy is a bigger drag than in the US, and the fiscal impulse that supported 2026 growth fades next year. Rates and FX markets have started to price this divergence, which GS says could be tricky to chase at current levels.

Brent risk is smaller: Gulf flows are back at pre-war levels and the market prices a risk premium GS estimates at $22/bbl for escalation. Risk is larger in refined products and natural gas, with LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz still very low ahead of winter.

A colder than average winter or stagnant supply could require TTF above 100 EUR/MWh to drive LNG demand destruction outside Europe and manage European gas inventories. Upside energy tails keep ECB hike pricing in check.

Past hiking cycles show peak terminal pricing about 3 months after peak core inflation. GS expects peak European core inflation around Q2 next year on the current energy path, which implies gradual ECB hikes if the Iran conflict continues. October ECB pricing has decayed to about 3bp, and the French and Italian spread moves raise the hurdle for faster hikes.
GS ran a poll this week showing opinions are divided on US long-end yield levels.

tension_points.bull_case: If AI ROI is easily double digits, a 50-100bp rise in funding cost does little to slow borrowing, and Nasdaq stays near highs with limited FCI tightening.
tension_points.bear_case: The supply/demand imbalance keeps pushing long-end yields up, hurting rate-sensitive sectors, small businesses and lower income quartiles in a K-shaped economy.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A repricing lower in the ROI of AI-related investment, or a sharper deterioration in parts of the K-shaped economy.

tension_points.bull_case: Fiscal support has underpinned European growth this year and ECB hikes may be gradual and measured.
tension_points.bear_case: Europe lags in AI growth benefits, sovereign spreads can widen and tighten FCI, energy is a bigger drag, and the fiscal impulse fades next year.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further sovereign spread widening in France or Italy, or TTF rising above 100 EUR/MWh in a cold winter.

theme_stances.key_argument: The sell-off is a supply/demand story driven by deficits and AI issuance, and it persists unless AI ROI is repriced or the cycle turns.
theme_stances.evidence: the longer term imbalance is likely to persist unless something changes

theme_stances.key_argument: The US is the clear AI winner while Europe lags and struggles in a high-rate world.
theme_stances.evidence: The US clearly stands out as one of the AI winners; Europe does not

theme_stances.theme: European energy risk and ECB hikes
theme_stances.key_argument: Upside risk to refined products and natural gas keeps ECB hike pricing in check, and hikes are likely gradual.
